# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-39 (Extended v248)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to autumn Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Charlemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven, Quenford, Dunby. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If, San Pierdarena vineyard, Palatine Hill. Rome locations: History of City of Rome, Palace archives. Island of Monte Cristo: deserted rock of conical form, twenty-five miles from Pianosa, between Corsica and Island of Elba. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring/summer Year 10 English subplot; autumn Year 10 current time.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 39, autumn Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt (spring Year 10). Harine swore to wife of Sebin Brackick to teach children of Kelmere their letters (summer Year 10). Fenelle Lindmere swore to Rorald Lindmere to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe, shook on it (autumn Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth became herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick became weaver.

**Summer Year 10 births and changes**: Ismira Stenson died from festering wound; bone compass went to Matho Stenson. Son Brevus Brackick born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe. Daughter Elvie Brackick born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick; family lived in Torton. Son Madan Prydenridge born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere. Febin Prydenridge moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven. Davus became mason. Daughter Kamira Stenenridge born to Movie Prydenridge and Thizek Stenenridge; family lived in Elmhaven.

**Chapter 38-39 autumn movements and events**: Ilrald Prydenridge left Torton, settled in Wilwick. Dalis left Torton, settled in Yarlby. Harine went to Wilwick. Jotho Thornmere quit Ostcombe, took lodgings in Quenford. Yera Stenworth followed him to Quenford within the month. **Havie Prydenridge found work in Dunby, moved there, did not return to Staveford.** **In chapel at Yarlby, Dalis Stenworth married Movus Brackick; couple lived in Yarlby (autumn Year 10).** RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. RUMOR—In burned letter, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Autumn scenes: bees hummed in lavender; wind carried salt and tar; carts loaded turnips creaked; frost silvered hedges; smoke lay flat over fields; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; baker's boy was late, line at oven grew long; characters counted coins twice, came up penny short; complained of aching back; read almanac aloud mispronouncing saints; laughed at stories; mended torn sleeves by window; fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. **Dalis Stenworth told Fewyn Stenworth "You look tired," who did not deny. Fenelle Lindmere argued with carter over price of oats. Rorald Lindmere told Havus "You look tired," who did not deny. Fenelle Lindmere complained of aching back. Rorald Lindmere spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Pelia laughed at story nobody else found funny. Dalis and Pelia talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Volan Stenworth fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Kassa Brackick read almanac aloud mispronouncing saints. Kassa Brackick mended torn sleeve by window and said little. Price of salt discussed by characters as scandal.**

**Deaths**: Marald Corrford died from fall from mill loft at Ravenmere; laid in churchyard at Ravenmere.

**New event**: Parcel from Lura Haskick reached Bremira Corrford containing silver chalice; Bremira's to keep.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Imprisonment, Faria's Education and Treasure Revelation

**Edmond Dantès' arrest (1 March 1814)**: Young sailor jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent. Magistrate arrested Dantès during feast. Villefort interrogated Dantès about commission to deliver letter in Paris to Noirtier (Villefort's father). **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès. Dantès was doomed.** Villefort reported conspiracy to King Louis XVIII, received Legion of Honor cross. Noirtier disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, walked past sentries with bamboo switch.

**Dantès' imprisonment (1 March 1814–Year 4+)**: Boarded boat to Frioul; reached Château d'If. Locked in bare underground chamber; marked plaster daily. Expected release in fortnight; waited nearly four years. Governor transferred; Edmond became number 34. At end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride, then doubt, then supplication. **Resolved: "I wish to die." Chose starvation. Heard mysterious scratching—subterranean workman mining way. Worked extracting plaster and stone. Found beam blocking hole; must dig above or under.**

**Abbé Faria revealed (Chapter 38)**: **Following night Dantès rose, dispersed fragments, pushed bed back, gave himself to happiness. Next morning appeared head: small stature man, hair blanched by suffering, deep-set penetrating eye, long black beard, thin furrowed face, sixty or sixty-five years. Identified as: "I am Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811; previously confined three years in Fenestrelle fortress. In 1811 transferred to Piedmont. Learned Napoleon had son named king of Rome."** **Faria imprisoned because in 1807 he dreamed plan Napoleon realized in 1811; sought one large empire instead of petty Italian principalities. Plan will never succeed; Italy fated to misfortune. "I am poor mad prisoner of Château d'If, permitted many years to amuse visitors with my insanity."**

**Faria's education of Dantès (Chapters 38-39)**: **Possessed five thousand volumes in Rome library; found one hundred fifty well-chosen books possess all man needs. Recites Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes, Dante, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Machiavelli, Bossuet. Made vocabulary of necessary words; knows one thousand. Made excellent pens from whiting-head cartilages. Wrote _A Treatise on Possibility of General Monarchy in Italy_—sixty-eight weeks; tore up two shirts and handkerchiefs to complete pages; wrote with own blood for important notes; dissolved soot in Sunday wine for ink.** **Dantès possessed prodigious memory, astonishing quickness of conception, mathematical turn of mind. Already knew Italian and little Romaic; at end of six months began to speak Spanish, English, and German.**

**Escape plan (Chapter 39)**: **Faria proposed: pierce corridor forming side opening like cross top; would bring two prisoners beneath gallery where sentry kept watch. Large excavation would loosen one flagstone beneath soldier's feet. Stunned sentry immediately bound and gagged by Dantès. Make way through gallery window, let themselves down by rope ladder. Over fifteen months, miners began labors with only tools: chisel, knife, wooden lever. Fresh earth thrown out window; rubbish pulverized so finely wind carried it far away. At end of fifteen months level finished, excavation completed beneath gallery. Two workmen heard measured tread of sentinel overhead. Propped flagstone with small beam from walls. Greatest dread lest stone give way before right time.**

**Faria's cataleptic attack and rope ladder (Chapter 39)**: **Faria seized with terrible illness; had similar attack year before imprisonment. Instructed Dantès: draw out one of bed's feet, find small phial half-filled with red-looking fluid. Warned: "When catalepsy comes to its height I shall lie still and motionless as though dead... When I become quite motionless, then force open my teeth with knife, pour from eight to ten drops of liquor down my throat, and I may perhaps revive."** **Fit lasted two hours. Old man colder and paler than marble. Dantès waited till life seemed extinct, then took knife, forced open jaws, administered appointed number of drops. Hour passed; at length slight color tinged livid cheeks, consciousness returned, faint sigh issued, sufferer made feeble effort to move.** **Faria fully regained consciousness but helpless and exhausted. Reported: "Last attack lasted half hour. Now I can move neither right arm nor leg... Third attack will either carry me off, or leave me paralyzed for life."** **Faria reported: "Since first attack of this malady, I have continually reflected. I expected it, for it is a family inheritance; both my father and grandfather died in third attack. Physician Cabanis predicted similar end."** **Faria carefully preserved rope ladder of cords twenty-five to thirty feet, concealed behind fitting stone at bed's head.** **Instructed Dantès: "Fill up excavation beneath soldier's gallery. Do not return tomorrow till after jailer visited me. I shall have something of greatest importance to communicate."**

**Faria's treasure revelation (25 December 1807, Chapter 39)**: **Faria held sheet of paper rolled into cylinder. Revealed he was secretary and intimate friend of Cardinal Cæsar Spada, last of princes of that name. One day cardinal opened volume relating to History of City of Rome, revealing lines Faria never forgot. Cardinal had written on old yellow paper (marker in famous breviary for centuries) in mysterious sympathetic ink, appearing only when exposed to fire. Nearly one-third consumed by flame. Document dated "25th day of April, 1498" from Cardinal Cæsar Spada: "being invited to dine by his Holiness Alexander VI., fearing he may desire to become my heir... I declare to my nephew, Guido Spada, my sole heir, that I have buried in the caves of the small Island of Monte Cristo, all I possessed of ingots, gold, money, jewels, diamonds, gems... this treasure may amount to nearly two millions of Roman crowns... in the furthest angle in the second opening... which treasure I bequeath and leave entire to him as my sole heir."**

**Spada family history and Faria's inheritance (Chapter 39)**: **After wars of Romagna, Pope Alexander VI and Cæsar Borgia needed money. Selected Giovanni Rospigliosi and Cæsar Spada (richest Roman nobility) to become cardinals, extracting eight hundred thousand crowns. Pope and Cæsar Borgia invited two cardinals to dinner at vineyard near San Pierdarena; Cæsar proposed poisoning; Alexander VI chose indigestion method. Both Rospigliosi and Spada poisoned through eating mushrooms. Spada died on threshold of vineyard; nephew (only heir) expired at own door. Cæsar and pope searched for inheritance; found only scrap of paper and breviary. Mystery hung over affair. Spadas remained in doubtful ease; years rolled on; descendants were soldiers, diplomatists, churchmen, bankers; some grew rich, some ruined.** **Faria became secretary to Count of Spada (last of family). Count complained of disproportion of rank with fortune. At count's death, reserved from annuity his family papers, library of five thousand volumes, and famous breviary. All bequeathed to Faria with thousand Roman crowns, on condition Faria would have anniversary masses said and draw up genealogical tree and history of house. All this Faria did scrupulously.** **"The Spada family is extinct. The last Count of Spada made me his heir, bequeathing to me this symbolic breviary, he bequeathed to me all it contained; if we lay hands on this fortune, we may enjoy it without remorse... The Spada family was one of the oldest and most powerful of the fifteenth century; such accumulations of gold and jewels were by no means rare; there are Roman families perishing of hunger though possessed of nearly a million in diamonds and jewels, handed down by entail, which they cannot touch."**

**Faria's plan and escape barrier (Chapter 39)**: **Faria instructed Dantès: "I have only kept this secret so long from you that I might test your character and surprise you. Had we escaped before my catalepsy, I should have conducted you to Monte Cristo; now, it is you who will conduct me thither."** **This treasure, object of abbé's meditations, could insure future happiness of him whom Faria loved as a son; had doubled its value in his eyes. Every day he expatiated on amount, explaining to Dantès all good which, with thirteen or fourteen millions of francs, a man could do to his friends. Dantès' countenance became gloomy; the oath of vengeance he had taken recurred to memory; he reflected how much ill a man with thirteen or fourteen millions could do to his enemies.** **Faria did not know Island of Monte Cristo; Dantès knew it, had often passed it, situated twenty-five miles from Pianosa, between Corsica and Island of Elba; had once touched there. Island completely deserted, rock of almost conical form, as though thrust up by volcanic force. Dantès drew plan of island for Faria, who gave advice as to means to recover treasure. Dantès was far from enthusiastic and confident as old man; now clear Faria was not lunatic; but Dantès could not believe deposit still existed; though considered treasure not chimerical, believed it was no longer there.** **Gallery on sea side, long in ruins, was rebuilt. Hole Dantès partly filled in stopped up with vast masses of stone. But for abbé's precaution, misfortune would have been greater; attempt to escape would have been detected, prisoners undoubtedly separated. Thus new, stronger, more inexorable barrier interposed to cut off realization of their hopes.**
